title: The Neuro-Cognitive Approach to Urban Planning: Wayfinding Behavior Analysis and its Effect on Urban Planning
central_proposition: The neuro-cognitive approach, utilizing tools like EEG and eye-tracking, provides quantitative insights into how specific urban design elements (such as street width, building height, geometry, and landmarks) influence human wayfinding behavior, cognitive states, and emotional responses, thereby offering a novel framework for urban planning and design.

concept_definitions.name: Urban Wayfinding
concept_definitions.definition: The achievement of an objective point or the directing of behavior in the physical environment, seen as an act of decision-making.

concept_definitions.name: Neuro-Cognitive Approach
concept_definitions.definition: An analytical method that examines the interactions of urban design with cognitive and behavioral aspects using neuro-cognitive tools (EEG, ET) to obtain quantitative results.

concept_definitions.name: Imageability
concept_definitions.definition: The quality of a physical environment that gives it a high probability of evoking a strong image in the observer.

concept_definitions.name: Landmark
concept_definitions.definition: Remarkable elements in the urban environment that attract direct attention and assist in wayfinding.

concept_definitions.name: Amorphous Geometry
concept_definitions.definition: Building designs that deviate from smooth or normal geometries, characterized by different textures and materials.

argument_structure: The paper argues that traditional urban design methods often overlook human psychological needs and visual aspects, leading to monotony and wayfinding difficulties. It proposes that a neuro-cognitive approach, by quantitatively measuring brain activity and eye movements in response to specific urban design elements, can reveal underlying cognitive and emotional mechanisms of wayfinding. This understanding can then inform more human-centered urban planning criteria. The study designs a virtual city with varied elements, collects neuro-cognitive data from participants navigating it, and analyzes these data to support its propositions about the impact of design on wayfinding.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic is that specific physical characteristics of the urban environment (antecedents) trigger distinct neuro-cognitive responses (mechanisms, e.g., changes in brainwave frequencies, gaze patterns) which, in turn, influence wayfinding behavior (consequents, e.g., time taken, perceived ease/difficulty, stress levels). Narrow streets lead to increased beta and alpha waves, indicating heightened stress and visual processing demands, resulting in weakened wayfinding. Wide streets allow for more gazes and fixations, implying easier visual processing and reduced stress. Landmarks increase gamma band activity and fixation duration, making them easier to identify and serving as effective wayfinding cues. Amorphous geometry increases alpha and beta waves, suggesting mental relaxation, arousal, and heightened mindfulness, which positively affects wayfinding. Intersections modulate alpha, theta, and delta oscillations, reflecting their role as critical decision-making points. Low buildings increase alpha wave strength, indicating increased emotional responses, relaxation, and attention, leading to easier wayfinding. Green areas promote mental rest and positive affect, leading to longer time spent.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Narrow street configurations will lead to increased beta and alpha brainwave activity (indicating stress and heightened visual processing) and longer wayfinding times compared to wide streets.
The presence of distinct landmarks will correlate with increased gamma band activity and longer fixation durations, and will facilitate wayfinding.

Urban areas with amorphous building geometries will elicit higher alpha and beta brainwave activity (indicating mental relaxation and mindfulness) and result in clearer, more stable wayfinding routes compared to areas with normal geometries.

Intersections will induce specific modulations in alpha, theta, and delta brainwave oscillations (indicating alertness and calm) and require longer fixation durations, reflecting their role as critical decision-making points.
Low-rise building environments will be associated with stronger alpha wave activity (indicating relaxation and positive emotional responses) and easier wayfinding compared to high-rise environments.
Green urban areas will be associated with longer time spent by individuals, reflecting their restorative qualities.
bridge_warrants: The study connects urban design principles (Lynch's imageability, Rapoport's characteristics) with neuro-cognitive responses, bridging traditional design theory with neuroscience.
It links wayfinding behavior to cognitive processes (attention, memory, decision-making) and emotional states (stress, relaxation).
It implicitly connects to Attention Restoration Theory (ART) and Stress Recovery Theory (SRT) through findings on green spaces and mental relaxation.
It connects to Predictive Processing by showing how environmental features (landmarks, geometry) reduce prediction error or manage cognitive load.
model_structure: The paper does not propose a formal model structure, but rather an approach that integrates Virtual Reality (VR), Electroencephalography (EEG), Eye-Tracking (ET), and custom software (Urban Activity Timer - UAT) to quantitatively analyze the neuro-cognitive effects of urban design elements on wayfinding. This approach can be seen as a methodological framework for future studies.
limitations: External factors such as light, ambient sound, and temperature were kept constant but can affect EEG data and cognitive activity, and should be considered in future research.
The EEG device used had only 14 channels; a higher channel count or fMRI could provide a more detailed analysis of brain activity.
The study was conducted in a virtual city, which may not fully replicate the complexities and sensory richness of real urban conditions, potentially limiting ecological validity.
